about: One man is written 'Dax Orlo' eight times and 'Dax' alone eleven times; the review must give both entries one gender and one spelling of the shared name.
title: The Harbour Office
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Morning
paragraphs: Dax Orlo arrived at the harbour office before dawn. He hung his wet coat on the nail by the door.
Ysolde was already there with the tide tables. She had marked three of them in red.
Dax read the first table slowly. He disliked red ink and said so.
The kettle began to sing. Ysolde took it off the stove and poured two cups.
Dax Orlo drank his tea standing up. He had never learned to sit while the harbour was awake.
Ysolde unrolled the chart. She pinned its corners with four brass weights.
Dax traced the channel with one finger. He stopped where the water turned pale.
The first boat of the morning nosed past the breakwater. Gulls rose and settled again.
Dax signalled from the window. He waved the red flag twice, slowly, as the rules required.
Ysolde noted the time in the log. She wrote small and straight, like her mother.
Dax Orlo kept the harbour office for thirty years. He knew every keel by its sound.
Ysolde brought him the second tide table. She did not argue about the ink this time.
Dax laughed at that. He had a short, dry laugh that startled the gulls.
By noon the fog had lifted and the water lay flat. Dax locked the cash box and wiped his hands.
Ysolde counted the day's fees. She entered them in the ledger and blotted the page.
Dax Orlo put on his coat again. He checked the nail twice before he left.
At the door Dax turned and looked back at the room. He nodded to Ysolde, who did not look up.
The harbour bell rang the half hour. Dax listened until the last note died.
Ysolde shut the ledger and set the kettle back on the stove. She waited for the next boat.
Dax came back at dusk with a parcel under his arm. He set it on the counter without a word.
Inside the parcel lay a small brass compass. Ysolde turned it over and read the maker's mark.
Dax Orlo said it had been his father's. He asked her to keep it on the chart table.
In the district everyone knew Dax Orlo, and nobody had a bad word for Dax Orlo.
Years afterwards people still asked about Dax Orlo, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Dax, and nobody had a bad word for Dax.
Years afterwards people still asked about Dax, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Ysolde, and nobody had a bad word for Ysolde.
Years afterwards people still asked about Ysolde, though few could say why.
